A.explanation: With $F = 1.6 \times 10^{-14} \text{ N}$ and $|q| = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ for an electron, $E = F/q = 1.0 \times 10^{5} \text{ V m}^{-1}$, not $5.0 \times 10^{5} \text{ V m}^{-1}$.

B.explanation: An alpha-particle has charge $2e = 3.2 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, so $E = 3.2 \times 10^{-14}/3.2 \times 10^{-19} = 1.0 \times 10^{5} \text{ V m}^{-1}$.

C.explanation: With $F = 8.0 \times 10^{-14} \text{ N}$ and $q = 3.2 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ for an alpha-particle, $E = 2.5 \times 10^{5} \text{ V m}^{-1}$, only half the required value.

D.explanation: With $F = 8.0 \times 10^{-14} \text{ N}$ and $q = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ for a proton, $E = 8.0 \times 10^{-14}/1.6 \times 10^{-19} = 5.0 \times 10^{5} \text{ V m}^{-1}$.

hints: Notice each option gives a force $F$ on a named particle, so you need the charge $q$ of an electron, proton and alpha-particle to find $E$.

Recall that electric field strength is force per unit charge, $E = F/q$, with $|q| = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ for electron and proton and $q = 3.2 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ for an alpha-particle.
Divide each $10^{-14} \text{ N}$ force by its particle charge and compare the result with $5.0 \times 10^{5} \text{ V m}^{-1}$.
walkthrough: Identify the rule for field strength: $E = F/q$, where $F$ is the electric force on charge $q$.
Recall the magnitudes of charge: electron $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, proton $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, alpha-particle $2e = 3.2 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$.
Set up the target: need $F/q = 5.0 \times 10^{5} \text{ V m}^{-1}$, so for charge $1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ the force must be $8.0 \times 10^{-14} \text{ N}$.
Check the proton case: $E = 8.0 \times 10^{-14} / 1.6 \times 10^{-19} = 5.0 \times 10^{5}$ with units $\text{N C}^{-1} = \text{V m}^{-1}$.
The other cases give $1.0 \times 10^{5}$, $1.0 \times 10^{5}$ and $2.5 \times 10^{5} \text{ V m}^{-1}$, so only the $8.0 \times 10^{-14} \text{ N}$ force on a proton matches. This is option D.
